edge.title: The holiday you pay for before you take it
edge.anchor: The Times of India reports a Bengaluru man paid ₹90,000 for a Country Vacations holiday membership and sought cancellation within six weeks without using any benefits; the NCDRC called the company's reliance on its 'no-refund' clause patently unfair.
edge.setup: A call says you have won a free stay or a gift voucher, and you only need to attend a short presentation with your spouse. Two hours in, after a nice lunch, the offer is a multi-year holiday membership at a 'today only' price, with an easy card swipe and a contract nobody has time to read.
edge.tell: The price is valid only in the room, and the contract only after you've paid.
move: Never sign or pay at the presentation. Ask for the full contract, cancellation and refund terms to take home; a real offer survives a night.
Read the cancellation and 'no-refund' clauses before paying anything, and check reviews and consumer-forum cases against the company's name.
If you have paid and want out, cancel in writing at once and keep proof. A 'no-refund' clause does not automatically bind you: Indian consumer forums have called such reliance unfair.
For a complaint, start with the National Consumer Helpline (1915) or e-daakhil.nic.in before going to the district consumer commission.
edge.why: The presentation is engineered so you decide while you're grateful for the free gift, tired, and told the price disappears at the door. Each pressure removes the one thing that protects you: time to compare. Anything that only works on a same-day decision is priced for people who did not compare.
edge.variants: Same shape: gym and club memberships sold on a 'founding member' price, 'free' skin or hair consultations that end in a package, timeshares, education courses with a 'scholarship' that expires tonight.

scenario.question: You and your partner get a call: you've won a free two-night resort stay, just attend a 90-minute presentation at a hotel. After lunch, the sales manager offers a 10-year holiday membership at ₹1.2 lakh, 'only for today's guests', and says you can pay a ₹20,000 deposit on your card now and read the papers at home. What do you do?

choices.text: Decline to pay anything today. Ask for the full contract and refund terms to take home, check consumer-forum cases against the company, and decide after comparing. If the price vanishes overnight, let it.
Pay the ₹20,000 deposit to lock in the price; you can always cancel later if the papers look bad.
Sign the full contract on EMI since the monthly amount is small and the free stay is already yours.

lens.name: Compounding
lens.one_line: Small consistent changes beat big sporadic ones, because the result is multiplicative, not additive.
lens.detail: Intuition is linear; compounding isn't, which is why almost everyone underestimates it. ₹5,000 a month at 12% is about ₹11 lakh in 10 years and roughly ₹50 lakh in 20 — most of that gain arriving in the final stretch. The same shape governs skills, reputation and debt. Credit-card interest at 3.5% a month is this force running against you at roughly 50% a year.
elsewhere: Minimum card payments keeping a balance alive for years.
Reputation: slow to build, then suddenly everything arrives at once.
lens.test: Is this a one-time event, or something that multiplies? Multiplying things deserve disproportionate attention.
lens.today: The Times of India reports Karnataka food inflation hit 12.16%, with milk, rice, pulses and oil driving Bengaluru grocery bills up. At that pace prices compound: a ₹10,000 monthly grocery bill becomes roughly ₹12,500 in two years if the rate holds. A salary hike or savings rate that does not beat it is quietly shrinking, so judge your increments against your own bill, not the headline number.

moved.what: The Times of India reports Karnataka food inflation has hit 12.16%, with milk, rice, pulses and oil pushing up Bengaluru grocery bills.
moved.so_what: Staples are what is rising, not treats. Stock up on non-perishables like rice, dal and oil when a store or app runs an offer, and compare per-kg prices rather than pack prices.

moved.what: Deccan Herald reports Karnataka has flagged petrol with up to 31% ethanol blending and asked for ethanol content to be disclosed on fuel bills.
moved.so_what: If your vehicle is older or not E20-rated, track your mileage over the next few fills. A sudden drop is a reason to change pumps, and keep your fuel bills in case disclosure becomes mandatory.

moved.what: Asianet Newsable reports Pink Line ridership is rising and Bannerghatta Road traffic is easing; BMTC has added 28 feeder buses across five new routes.
moved.so_what: If you drive on Bannerghatta Road, the easing is partly because others switched. Try one week of metro plus feeder bus and compare door-to-door time before traffic fills back in.

moved.what: Bengaluru's police has been reorganised into five commissionerates under a new chief commissioner, R Hithendra, Deccan Herald and The Hindu report.
moved.so_what: If you have an open complaint or FIR, note your station's new commissionerate and save the zonal contacts once published, so escalation does not stall during the handover.

carry_over.prompt: A clean two-year-old scooter at a fair price, low odometer, 'single owner', service booklet photos, and a ₹5,000 token wanted today because another buyer is coming; what is the tell?
carry_over.answer: Every claim is from the seller's mouth; none is from a record you fetched yourself.
